items.title: Most adult humans can't digest milk — and that's normal
items.claim: Babies make lactase to digest lactose in milk. In most of the world's adults, lactase production switches off after weaning. Adult milk-drinkers — common in Europeans and some African and Middle Eastern populations — carry a recently evolved mutation.

options.text: Adult lactose intolerance is ancestral; lactase persistence is a derived trait that arose in populations that domesticated dairy animals in the last 10,000 years

items.reveal:
Roughly 65 percent of adult humans globally show reduced lactase production after weaning. Lactase persistence is most common in northern Europeans (around 90 percent), some West African pastoralist groups, and some Middle Eastern populations.

Different regulatory mutations independently produced this trait in different lineages — convergent evolution. The European variant (a single nucleotide change near the LCT gene, called T-13910) is dated to about 5,000 to 10,000 years ago, coinciding with cattle domestication.

Dairy farming and lactase persistence appear to have co-evolved: ancient DNA shows farmers drank milk before persistence was common, suggesting cultural use (fermented dairy, lower lactose) preceded biological adaptation. As populations relied more on milk, the persistence allele was strongly selected.
items.why: European diets are taken as a baseline; lactose intolerance is treated as a disorder. Globally, lactose intolerance IS the baseline — milk drinking adults are the rare ones.

items.title: You synthesise your body weight in ATP every day
items.claim: ATP is the cell's energy currency. Your body contains only about 50 grams at any moment, but you turn it over so fast that you make and consume the equivalent of your full body mass — 60 to 80 kilograms — daily.
items.prompt: How can a tiny pool turn over so much?

options.text: Each ATP molecule is hydrolysed and re-synthesised hundreds of times per day; mitochondria continuously rebuild ATP from ADP and inorganic phosphate using the proton motive force from respiration
Most of the body's mass is ATP
ATP is consumed only during exercise

items.reveal:
An adult at rest uses about 2000 kcal per day. Each ATP hydrolysis releases ~7.3 kcal/mol of free energy under standard conditions, more under cellular conditions.

Working through: ~65 kg of ATP cycled per day, give or take. Each molecule of ATP cycles roughly 1000-1500 times daily.

The cell stores essentially no ATP for emergencies. It maintains a flux instead. Stop respiration and your ATP pool depletes in seconds — which is exactly why cyanide is so fast.

Muscles store some quick-access energy as phosphocreatine (a few seconds of all-out sprint) and glycogen (~minutes), but ATP itself is continuously regenerated, not stockpiled.

This is metabolism's deep design choice: a small, dynamic currency pool, refilled by continuous oxidation of food.
items.why: Energy storage feels like the obvious solution. Cells went the other way — keep almost no ATP, rebuild it constantly. The flux IS the metabolism.
